nameStory: The Ivory Gull gets its name from its stunning pure white plumage that resembles polished ivory. Unlike most gulls that sport gray backs and wings, adult Ivory Gulls are completely white from head to tail, making them look like living sculptures carved from precious ivory.
description: The Ivory Gull is a small, ethereally beautiful seabird that's pure white all over when fully mature. It's one of the most northerly-dwelling gulls in the world, breeding in the high Arctic of Greenland and northern Canada. These compact gulls are smaller than the familiar Herring Gulls you see along New England coasts. In New England, they're extremely rare visitors, with only 23 recorded sightings, making any encounter truly special.

idTips.label: Pure white plumage
idTips.description: Adults are completely white from head to toe - no gray on the back or wings like other gulls. The white appears almost luminous against gray skies, like fresh snow in sunlight.

idTips.label: Compact size
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller and more delicate than common gulls like Herring or Ring-billed Gulls, with a rounder head and shorter, stubbier bill.

idTips.label: Dark legs and bill tip
idTips.description: Yellow to greenish legs contrast sharply with the white body, and the bill often has a dark tip that looks like it was dipped in ink.

idTips.label: Rounded wings
idTips.description: Wings appear broader and more rounded than typical gulls, giving them a softer, almost dove-like flight silhouette.

idTips.label: Juvenile markings
idTips.description: Young birds show scattered black spots on their white plumage, like someone flicked ink from a pen, especially on wing tips and face.

habitat: In New England, Ivory Gulls are exceptionally rare winter visitors, most likely spotted along rocky coastlines, harbors, or fishing ports during harsh winter storms. They prefer areas with pack ice and may follow ice floes southward, so look for them during particularly cold winters when ice extends further south than usual.

seasonality.spring: Extremely rare; any sightings would likely be stragglers heading back north as ice begins to break up.
seasonality.summer: Virtually never seen in New England during summer months, as they're nesting in the high Arctic.
seasonality.fall: Very rare fall migrants might appear in late fall as Arctic ice begins forming, usually during severe weather systems.
seasonality.winter: Most likely season for sightings, though still extremely rare. Look during harsh winter storms or when unusual ice conditions push them south.

funFact: Ivory Gulls are sometimes called "ice partridges" because they follow polar bears across the Arctic ice, feeding on scraps from seal kills - they're essentially the polar bear's personal cleanup crew, living farther north than almost any other bird on Earth.
confusionNotes: Young Ivory Gulls with black markings might be confused with other young gulls, but the overall white appearance and compact size are distinctive. Adult Ivory Gulls are virtually unmistakable - no other gull in New England is pure white all over.
contextualKnowledge: Ivory Gulls are considered one of the "Holy Grail" birds for New England birders due to their extreme rarity. Climate change is affecting their Arctic habitat significantly, making southern sightings even more unusual and potentially concerning from a conservation perspective.
compareHints: As the only species in its genus, the Ivory Gull is unique among gulls. Compared to other small gulls like Bonaparte's or Black-headed Gulls, it's the only one that's completely white as an adult. Even compared to leucistic (abnormally white) individuals of other gull species, Ivory Gulls have a distinctive compact build and different proportions that set them apart.
